Conventional Radiology of the Digestive Tract Methods, Semiology, Pathology #1

  • Dr.Mihai Socaciu

There is no natural contrast inside the digestive tract #2

There is no natural contrast inside the digestive tract 1. Radioopaque substances: Ba Sulfate Hydrosoluble Iodine-based contrast agents - hyperosmolar, ionized (Gastrografin): in upper digestive tract perforations - hypoosmolar, non-ionized (Ultravist, Omnipaque, Iopamiro): in angiography, when one suspects fistulae - isoosmolar (Isovist) 2. Radiolucent substances (gas): Effervescent tablets (CO2 build-up): aesofagus, stomach Air or CO2 : colon exploration #3

Monocontrast - Duble contrast #4

Protocol - mandatory! #5

  • History and clinical exam: contraindications!!
  • “Plain” abdominal X-ray
  • Contrast exploration

Indications and Contraindications of a Barium Examination: Indications: Findings of pathological or possibly pathological conditions of the digestive tract during other imaging procedures => assessment of the movements of the digestive tract Postoperative assessment of the morphology and dynamics of digestive segments (Radioscopy still represents the best method of physiological assessment) Assessment of chronic digestive tract diseases (suspicion of malformations, Inflammatory Bowel Disease, ulcers, bowel tumors etc.) #6

B. Contraindications for Ba examinations: B.1. Absolute: suspicion of gastro-intestinal perforation intestinal occlusion B.2. Relative: recent gastrointestinal hemorrhage acute digestive diseases pregnancy (esp. in the first 3 mo) altered general state #7

2. Native (“plain”) radiologic examination of the abdomen. Main purpose: quick diagnosis of acute conditions contraindications of Ba administration associated abdominal pathology or complications #8

Slide 9 #9

Plain abdominal radiography/scopy (2) #10

  • Is the elective method in diagnosing pneumoperitoneum in orthostatic (standing) position
  • Whenever there is a suspicion of bowel perforation and/or peritonitis
  • Brings information concerning just the nature not the location of the pathological process (which could be diagnosed after Gastrografin Rx)

0 #11

Plain abdominal radiography/scopy (3) #12

  • Main examination in occlusions
  • Its roles are:
  • pozitive diagnosis
  • differential diagnosis between the mechanical and paralytic ileus
  • establishment of the level of occlusion (mechanical obstructions),
  • severity assessment (complications)
  • the nature of the obstacle (when possible)

Intestinal Occlusion #13

  • Pozitive diagnosis
  • Evidence of hydro-aeric levels (could be missing – false negative Dx).
  • In dynamic ileuses, the distention by gas is the main component, in mechanical ileuses the liquid buildup is the main component.

Slide 14 #14

Additionally, the presence in a certain quadrant of one or several (few) distended loops with hydro-aeric level, could add (along with the clinical signs) to a diagnosis of a special dynamic ileus: the sentinel loop ! #15

Slide 16 #16

Sentinel loops #17

  • colecystitis
  • apendicytis
  • Ulcer, pancreatitis
  • diverticulitis
  • Ulcer, lithiasis

Small bowel vs. Large bowel ? #18

Other changes visible on plain abdominal radiography #19

  • Pneumonic infiltrates
  • Thoracic Dissecting Aortic Aneurysm
  • Aspiration pneumonia
  • Pleural effusion
  • Subfrenic abscesses
  • Radioopaque stones (urinary, billiary)
  • Pancreatic calcifications
  • Calcified atheromas
  • Calcified lymph nodes
  • Tumor masses with calcifications (including hydatid cysts)
  • Feces and coprolites
  • Aerobilia
  • Characteristic signs of mesenteric infarction (intestinal pneumatosis, presence of air in the portal vein and bowel walls thickening)

Slide 20 #20

Preparation for the radiological examination of the bowel 1. Bowel preparation per se Upper GI tract: NO food, liquids or smoking in the morning of the examination. Time of examination: best between 8-10 a.m. (to prevent gastric hypersecretion due to hunger) Evacuation of stasis liquid for patients with gastric stasis Small Bowel: Hydric diet and purgatives in the day of examination Colon: Fasting, purgation (the day before) + high evacuation enemas 2. Premedication with farmacodynamic substances They have specific indications in the exploration of the small bowel. Are either hypotonic (glucagon or methylscopolamin), or accelerate the intestinal transit (metoclopramid). #21

Semiology of monocontrast Rx #22

  • Basic semiology notions required for the clinician in order to understand the common terms from forms
  • Morphology:
  • Location
  • Form and Dimension
  • * Contour:
  • incision, protrusion
  • addition images (ulcer, diverticulum, fistula),
  • substraction images = filling defects (lacunar, semitone, lucent halo around ulcers)
  • Internal texture (benign, malignant)
  • Degree of opacity

Semiology of monocontrast Rx #23

  • Dynamics:
  • - Tonus
  • - Hypotonic
  • - Hypertonic
  • - Spasm
  • - Rigidity
  • - Peristaltism
  • - Filling
  • - Secretion
  • - Evacuation

Semiology of monocontrast Rx #24

  • The INCISION (notch, cleft):
  • an image entering a cavitary organ under a sharp angle. May be due to organic or functional causes

Semiology of monocontrast Rx #25

  • PROTRUSION (boulge):
  • an image entering a cavitary organ under an obtuse (often hemispheric) angle. May be due to organic or functional causes

Semiology of monocontrast Rx #26

  • RIGIDITY:
  • the lack of flexibility in a portion or in the whole cavitary organ, manifesting through the absence of peristalsis in the affected area. May be due to organic or functional causes

Semiology of monocontrast Rx #27

  • ULCER:
  • the radiological image produced by a circumscribed tissue loss inside the wall of the tract. By filling with Ba (or other positive contrast agents), it looks like a rounded superimposed opacity on the frontal projection, or an opaque prominence outside the contour of the organ on the lateral projection.

Semiology of monocontrast Rx #28

  • DIVERTICULUM (pouch):
  • a circumscribed ectasy of the wall, which can contain all the layers (true diverticulum) or, frequently, just the mucosa and submucosa herniated through a lax muscular layer. On frontal projection appears as a round superimposed opacity while on lateral projection, as an opaque prominence outside the contour, which, characteristically preserves the mucosal relief. They frequently appear at the level of the esophagus, 2nd part of duodenum and colon. When large, it can contain a HA level.

Semiology of monocontrast Rx #29

  • FISTULAE :
  • addition images on the outer border of the tract, expending on variable distances as a result of discontinuity of ALL the layers. They can end blindly (“finger-in-glove”), communicate with other organs, with the peritoneal cavity or open trough the skin.
  • When suspecting fistulae, one must not administer Ba!
  • In the esotracheal fistula one must not administer Gastrografin!

Semiology of monocontrast Rx #30

  • LACUNA:
  • is a radiolucent image produced by the dislodgement of the contrast agent by a mass. It can be transient or fixed, benign (polyp), malignant, caused by alimentary waste or lucent foreign bodies. It can be also produced by excess gases, giving false images.

Semiology of monocontrast Rx #31

  • the SEMITONE:
  • is a radiolucent inhomogeneous image found at the border of a malignant lacunar image. It is produced by the dislodgement of contrast trough the “cauliflower” shaped projections of the tumor.

Semiology of monocontrast Rx #32

  • the LUCENT HALO:
  • is a radiolucent image surrounding an ulcer, which appears as a dislodgement of contrast by the surrounding edema or by tumor infiltration. Can appear homogeneous or inhomogeneous and differs according to the projection (front or lateral)

  • ACHALASIA

ACHALASIA #37

  • DEFINITION:
  • incomplete relaxation or lack of relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) during deglutition
  • absence of primary peristaltic waves in the lower 2/3
  • hypertonic LES at rest
  • FUCTIONAL CHANGES
  • lack of peristalsis in the lower 2/3 of the esophagus
  • non-peristaltic, non-propulsive contractions
  • absence of LES relaxation – short axial stenosis: “bird beak” appearence
  • - lack of the stomach gas bubble, HA level in the esophagus
  • - sedimentation of Ba and food
  • ORGANIC CHANGES
  • esophageal dilation (megaesophagus)
  • lengthening of the esophagus (megadolicoesophagus)
